candidates.name: d3r4A
candidates.idea: Keep the height and country widths that preserve whole tokens, widen Name enough for Guangzhou, and retain a floor width that supports coherent parentheticals. Recover space from City and Year to give comments 10px more than in d3r2B; check the rendered result for rounding and wrapping.
candidates.label: acceptable

whys: All columns fit and words remain intact, but narrow names and comments create frequent short lines. Long comments make some rows very tall, leaving large empty areas across the numeric columns.

The structure and numerical fields are intact, but the narrower name and comments columns create more fragmented phrases and taller rows. 'Mecca Royal Clock Tower' occupies four lines, and the long comments are especially choppy.

All columns fit and words remain intact, but the narrow name column breaks Mecca Royal Clock Tower into four lines and even CITIC Tower into two. Long comments create especially tall rows and interrupt scanning.

candidates.name: d1r4A
candidates.idea: Give city and floors enough width to address the observed word and parenthesis breaks, while retaining the whole numerical values and using the remaining space for comments.
candidates.label: gold

whys: The wider comments column improves sentence flow and reduces several tall rows, while heights and years remain easy to scan. Names still wrap heavily, and the narrow floors column separates some parenthetical quantities awkwardly.

The wider comments column gives the prose more natural lines and reduces several long rows while keeping headers and figures intact. Names remain narrow, however, and some floor entries split immediately after the plus sign.

The wider comments column gives prose more natural lines and reduces several tall rows while keeping the height values easy to scan. Names still wrap heavily, and some floor counts break just after the plus sign.

candidates.name: contrast
candidates.idea: Equal widths give excessive space to rank and short numeric values while leaving too little for building names, cities and comments. Long words would have to break or overflow, and comments would become difficult to read.
candidates.label: bad

whys: Equal columns waste space on rank and numeric fields while splitting names, cities, the Comments header and many words. Very tall rows make scanning and comparing buildings difficult.

The table fits and its grid remains intact, but equal widths force breaks inside names, cities, countries, comments, and the Comments header. Very tall rows and narrow text columns make reading and comparing entries difficult.

The grid fits, but equal columns split names, cities, countries and the Comments header inside words. Extremely narrow comments produce long vertical stacks and vast empty areas, making lookup and comparison laborious.

The wider name column keeps names such as CITIC Tower together, while comments wrap somewhat more comfortably than in A. Long notes still produce tall rows and substantial empty space around the comparison fields.

The table fits, headers and figures remain intact, and words do not break internally. The name column preserves 'Mecca Royal Clock' and 'CITIC Tower' better than B or D, but comments wrap into narrow blocks and produce tall, uneven rows.
The table fits and preserves whole words, with clear height columns. Long names and comments wrap heavily, and tall comment-driven rows leave large empty areas across the numerical columns.

d1.purpose: Present a ranked reference list of tall buildings with their dimensions, locations, completion years and contextual notes.
tasks: Find a building by rank or name and read across its row.
Compare heights and floor counts between buildings.
Identify buildings by city and country or check their completion years.
Read the ranking sequentially and consult comments for context.
relations: Each row connects one building to its measurements, location, year and comments.
The metre and foot columns are two representations of the same height and sit under a shared header.
City and country jointly identify the location; floor-count qualifiers belong with their counts.
roles: The first column carries the rank, and the name column identifies the building.
Height and floors support numerical comparison; year supports chronological lookup.
City and country provide geographic context, while comments contain longer explanatory text.
The two-level header groups the height units without adding a separate data row.
keep_whole: Ranks, height values, years and individual words or numeric units.
Building names and place names should remain recognizable when they wrap.
Floor counts and their below-ground qualifiers should remain easy to associate.
may_wrap: Building names and multiword city or country names at word boundaries.
Floor-count qualifiers and comments at natural phrase or word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height columns should be nearly equal in width because they carry equivalent measurements.
City and country should have comparable prominence, adjusted for their different content.
Rank and year are compact lookup fields; names and comments need more space for text.
d1.h_vs_v: Fitting nine columns into 719px requires substantial vertical expansion. Preserving complete words and compact numerical columns leaves a limited shared budget for names, locations, floor qualifiers and comments; allocating it differently changes which rows become tallest.

d2.purpose: Present a ranked reference list of the tallest buildings, with dimensions, location, completion year and explanatory comments.
tasks: Identify a building by rank or name.
Compare heights and floor counts across buildings.
Find a building’s location and completion year.
Read comments for context and qualifications.
relations: Each row describes one building; rank, name and height are the main comparison path.
The m and ft columns are two units for the same height and belong under a shared header.
City and country jointly identify location; floor-count notes qualify the count.
roles: The first column is an unlabeled rank indicator; Name identifies the building.
Height has a grouped header and two unit subheaders; Floors, City, Country and Year are attributes.
Comments carry longer explanatory text and can dominate row height.
The two header rows establish the column hierarchy; body rows should remain easy to follow across the table.
keep_whole: Rank numbers, height values, floor counts, years and individual words.
The m and ft unit labels and the association of each floor count with its below-ground qualifier.
may_wrap: Multiword cities and countries at word boundaries.
Floor-count qualifiers and comments at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height columns should have nearly equal widths because they contain parallel measurements.
Rank and year should remain compact; name, location and comments need space according to their content rather than equal widths.
d2.h_vs_v: The 719px limit leaves little room beyond the longest unbreakable units, so wrapping and taller rows are unavoidable. Extra width can reduce wrapping in names, floor qualifiers or comments, but giving it to one increases vertical density elsewhere.

d3.purpose: Provide a ranked reference for comparing the world's tallest buildings and identifying their locations and characteristics.
tasks: Find a building or rank and read across its row.
Compare heights, floor counts and completion years.
Locate buildings by city and country and consult the comments for context.
relations: The metre and foot values are equivalent measurements under the shared Height header.
City and country jointly identify location.
Floor counts may include a parenthetical below-ground count.
Comments qualify or add context to individual buildings.
roles: The first column carries rank; Name identifies the building.
Height, Floors and Year provide compact comparison values.
City and Country provide location; Comments contains explanatory prose.
The two-level header groups the height units while the other headers span both header rows.
keep_whole: Rank numbers, individual height values and years.
Individual words and numeric tokens in names, locations, floor counts and comments.
The m and ft unit headers.
may_wrap: Multiword building names, cities and countries at word boundaries.
Floor-count parentheticals and comments at natural word boundaries.
same_scale: The two height-unit columns should be similarly narrow.
Rank and year are compact lookup fields; name and comments need more space for longer text.
d3.h_vs_v: The viewport is too narrow to keep all content on one line. Compact numeric columns preserve comparison, while widths assigned to names, floor descriptions and comments trade horizontal space against taller rows.

analysis.strengths: The wider Comments column gives several long notes more natural breaks and makes the table 93 px shorter than Q. Names, cities, numbers and headers remain legible without measured breaks inside words.
analysis.faults: At 720 px, the measured table exceeds the 719 px limit by 1 px. Several names and floor descriptions still occupy three or four lines, and long comments create tall rows with considerable empty space in adjacent columns.
analysis.spatial_logic: P keeps the numeric columns close to their content requirements, gives City enough room for its longest unbreakable name, and directs much of the remaining width to Comments.

analysis.strengths: The table fits within the width limit. Headers and numeric values remain on one line, and the slightly wider Floors and Country columns give those fields a little more room.
analysis.faults: The narrower Comments column produces more fragmented notes and adds 93 px to the table height. The extra width given to Floors and Country does not visibly compensate for the longer comment-driven rows.
analysis.spatial_logic: Q reserves more space for several short factual columns and leaves 8 px unused relative to the width limit, reducing the space available for continuous prose.

rounds.insights: Comments are the main driver of row height, so a small width change there can affect the whole table. The building names are also important lookup anchors and remain cramped in both layouts. Rank, height and year need little spare width, while City must accommodate long single words. P shows the stronger prose allocation, but Q is the only shown layout that meets the stated width limit.

bad.why: Its measured table width is 720px, exceeding the 719px fit limit. The wider comments column improves several rows, but the rendered table fails the stated constraint.

contrast.why: Equal widths give excessive space to rank and short numeric values while leaving too little for building names, cities and comments. Long words would have to break or overflow, and comments would become difficult to read.

sameFunctionGroups.why: Both columns express building height in different units and have nearly identical content widths; their nearly equal widths support comparison.
City and country both identify location, but their text lengths differ. They need enough room for their own content rather than equal widths.

synthesis.rationale: Q fits within the stated limit, keeps the headers on one line and shows no measured breaks inside words. Its narrow comments column makes several rows tall, while names and floor descriptions also wrap heavily. P improves the comments but its measured width exceeds the fit limit by 1px.

general: Allocate width according to content and reading task, preserving complete numeric values and avoiding breaks inside words.
Judge the rendered table against the actual width constraint and inspect how wrapping affects lookup and row height.
specific: The two height units need similar compact widths, while comments benefit from the remaining space.
The floor descriptions contain parenthetical text, so their width affects readability even though the leading floor counts are short.

synthesis.tradeoffs: Q sacrifices continuous reading in comments and building names to keep every column visible within the viewport. P reduces some comment wrapping and overall height, but its measured width exceeds the permitted table width.
synthesis.uncertain: The reported widths for P sum to 719px, while its measured rendered table is 720px. The rendered measurement governs this judgment; a revised P would need to be rendered and checked again.
